title: Rep. Meredith R. Lawson-Rowe voted Yea on SB450, a capital appropriations bill
text:
Rep. Meredith R. Lawson-Rowe voted Yea on SB450, a capital appropriations bill
State Rep. Meredith R. Lawson-Rowe (D-5th) voted Yea on SB450, a capital appropriations bill, which passed the Ohio House 95-3 during the 136th Ohio General Assembly on Wednesday, June 10, 2026, according to the Ohio Legislature.
The following summary and breakdown are based on the bill's official text and may include interpretation to clarify the bill's provisions.
This bill makes capital appropriations through June 30, 2028, and adjusts related statutes to finance state and local infrastructure, education, natural resources, and community facilities, while declaring an emergency for immediate effect. It expands and restructures bond-issuing authority and debt service mechanisms, including for state capital improvements, Clean Ohio conservation projects, school facilities, higher education, parks, and correctional and behavioral health facilities. The bill creates an aging school accelerator pilot program, requires Central State University to shift facilities management to another governmental entity as a condition for major renovations, and refines rules for allocating public works, Clean Ohio, and capital loan funds.
SB450 was introduced by Sen. Jerry C. Cirino.
Lawson-Rowe is serving her first term in the Ohio House of Representatives, representing the 5th House District. She previously made history as one of the first Black women elected to Reynoldsburg City Council in 2019 and was elected Council President in 2023.
Lawson-Rowe attended Clark Atlanta University, where she became a member of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc.
She has sponsored over a dozen pieces of legislation in the Ohio House, including Avery's Law, which was signed into law in December 2025.
In Ohio, the legislative process begins when a bill is introduced in either the House of Representatives or the Senate. A bill must receive three considerations in each chamber, and it may be referred to a committee for hearings, debate and possible amendments before advancing to a floor vote. If both chambers pass the same version, the bill is sent to the governor, who can sign it, veto it or allow it to become law without a signature. The Ohio General Assembly begins a new legislative session every two years on the first Monday in January of odd-numbered years, and there is no limit on the number of days it may convene.
